title: Ride-hailing driver matching
prompt: Design driver matching for a ride-hailing app in one large region. 500,000 drivers are online at peak, and each driver's phone sends its location every 4 seconds. Riders request about 50,000 rides an hour at peak, and each request should be offered to a nearby available driver within 5 seconds. A driver must never be offered two rides at once, and a ride must never go to two drivers. Once matched, the rider watches the driver's car move on a map.
explanation: The volume is in location updates, 125,000 a second, but each one is disposable; the correctness is in matching, a handful of requests a second that must never double-assign. Strong answers split the two and use a geospatial index for nearby.

requirements: Covers location updates, matching a request to a nearby available driver, and live tracking for the rider
Puts numbers on matching time (5 seconds) and on how stale a driver's location may be
Makes one ride per driver and one driver per ride an explicit correctness requirement
estimation: 125,000 location updates a second (500,000 drivers ÷ 4 seconds)
Current positions are only about 50 MB, so they fit in memory, and ride requests are only about 14 a second
Keeping every location point would be about 1 TB a day, so history goes to cheap storage, off the hot path
api_data_model: A location update (driver id, latitude, longitude, timestamp, status) and a ride request returning a ride id
A geospatial index of available drivers by cell (geohash, S2 or H3), held in memory
Rides with a state machine: requested, offered, accepted, en route, completed or cancelled
architecture: A location service that feeds updates into the in-memory geo index, separate from the matching service
Matching searches nearby cells, ranks candidates by ETA, and offers to one driver at a time with a timeout
Live tracking pushes the assigned driver's position to the rider over a WebSocket
scalability: Shards the geo index by cell so updates and searches spread across nodes
Handles dense city-centre cells with smaller cells or by splitting hot cells
Writes location history asynchronously through a stream such as Kafka, off the matching path
reliability: Claims a driver atomically when offering (compare-and-set on driver status) so two requests cannot take one driver
Times out an unanswered offer and moves on to the next driver
Treats locations as soft state that the next update rebuilds within 4 seconds, so losing a node is survivable
communication: Follows one ride request from the rider's tap to a driver accepting it
Keeps the high-volume location stream clearly apart from the low-volume, correctness-critical matching flow
